account: Noland Arbaugh, paralyzed after a diving accident, received the Neuralink N1 implant at Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, in January 2024 (ABC15, 2 May 2024). He demonstrated online chess and cursor movement by thought. Tech Times later reported that roughly 85% of the implant's threads retracted from his brain about a month after surgery. ABC News reported on 17 May 2024 that threads had retracted and that removal was considered. It quoted him: “I can control a computer just like anyone else can”. Neuralink said that it modified the recording algorithm and the translation of signals into cursor movements. Nature news reported on 6 August 2024 that the device “has been adjusted in a bid to prevent glitches”. The Debrief counted 7 users on 7 July 2025, 6 of them implanted at Barrow. Sky News reported on 29 January 2026 that its science editor watched a UK trial participant, who received the implant at University College London Hospital, move a cursor by thought. The same report states that results from the trials had not yet been published in peer-reviewed journals or submitted to regulators. Tech Times reports that by early 2026 the trial had enrolled more than 20 participants across sites in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the United Arab Emirates. Barrow reported on 29 April 2026 that the second participant, Alex Conley, controls a robotic arm to operate light switches and doors. Conley has a C4-C5 spinal cord injury and takes part in the CONVOY study. Tech Times reported on 28 May 2026, 28 months after the surgery, that software refinement had restored Arbaugh's use after the retraction. Citing an earlier report, Tech Times gave about 10 hours of daily use for chess, coursework, scheduling and communication.

Outcomes rest on the participant's own account, Barrow's patient story and press reports, not on a peer-reviewed report.

He demonstrated online chess and cursor movement by thought. ABC News (17 May 2024) reported that threads retracted from his brain and removal was considered. fields.account: Noland Arbaugh, paralyzed after a diving accident, received the Neuralink N1 implant at Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, in January 2024 (ABC15, 2 May 2024). He demonstrated online chess and cursor movement by thought. Tech Times later reported that roughly 85% of the implant's threads retracted from his brain about a month after surgery. ABC News reported on 17 May 2024 that threads had retracted and that removal was considered. It quoted him: “I can control a computer just like anyone else can”. Neuralink said that it modified the recording algorithm and the translation of signals into cursor movements. Nature news reported on 6 August 2024 that the device “has been adjusted in a bid to prevent glitches”. The Debrief counted 7 users on 7 July 2025, 6 of them implanted at Barrow. Sky News reported on 29 January 2026 that its science editor watched a UK trial participant, who received the implant at University College London Hospital, move a cursor by thought. The same report states that results from the trials had not yet been published in peer-reviewed journals or submitted to regulators. Tech Times reports that by early 2026 the trial had enrolled more than 20 participants across sites in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the United Arab Emirates. Barrow reported on 29 April 2026 that the second participant, Alex Conley, controls a robotic arm to operate light switches and doors. Conley has a C4-C5 spinal cord injury and takes part in the CONVOY study. Tech Times reported on 28 May 2026, 28 months after the surgery, that software refinement had restored Arbaugh's use after the retraction. Citing an earlier report, Tech Times gave about 10 hours of daily use for chess, coursework, scheduling and communication.
fields.summary: Neuralink's N1 implant and its decoding software let Noland Arbaugh, paralyzed after a diving accident, control a computer by thought, and he still used it 28 months after surgery.
